content: Social workers and client managers, often originating from key population communities, are regularly trained in human rights, ethics, and innovative approaches to working with target groups. AFEW organizes national and regional workshops and mass events to facilitate the sharing of experiences and best practices among key populations. Participants in these programs have reported improved collaboration and integration of services as a result of AFEW's initiatives. However, the requirement for a local residency permit remains a significant barrier to accessing care for key populations. To address this, NGOs like AFEW have signed memoranda of understanding with local providers to ensure access to essential services for those without residency permits. The Egyptian Family Planning Association (EFPA) extends its clinical services through outreach programs targeting young people at high risk of HIV. Volunteer peer educators provide comprehensive, gender-sensitive, rights-based sexual and reproductive health education. Each clinic employs two male and two female educators aged 18–25, trained in sexual and reproductive health (SRH), HIV, other STIs, and communication skills. These educators are supervised by clinic staff and EFPA reproductive health and youth officers. Of the 56 EFPA educators, 30 are specifically trained to work with young key populations, with some being members of these populations themselves. Outreach sessions are conducted with young people under 18, primarily in government institutions for street children and orphanages, at locations away from clinics to maintain confidentiality. Educators explain clinic services, encourage attendance, and distribute condoms. Outreach also targets young key populations not connected to institutions, such as truck and minibus drivers. In 2012, 81 peer-to-peer sessions reached nearly 2,300 individuals, one-third of whom were men who have sex with men (MSM) or young people who inject drugs. A youth committee meets quarterly to review activities, address obstacles, and share lessons learned. EFPA also advocates for policy changes prioritizing SRH needs of young people within the national health system. In India, the Pehchan program, implemented by the India HIV/AIDS Alliance and consortium partners, operates in 17 states to strengthen the capacity of 200 community-based organizations (CBOs) to deliver HIV prevention programs to over 450,000 MSM, transgender people, and hijras (collectively referred to as MTH populations). Pehchan develops CBOs as implementing partners with the National AIDS Control Programme, promotes community-friendly health services, and engages in advocacy to improve the lives of MTH populations. The program complements the government’s HIV prevention strategy by providing additional services that foster an enabling environment for healthy behaviors. Partnerships with the government are crucial for national-scale programming. Pehchan has addressed critical gaps in community capacity, enabling significant HIV prevention coverage for MTH populations. Active involvement of MTH community members as program managers and technical advisors has built trust and fostered community ownership. However, societal attitudes against homosexuality in India, exacerbated by the re-criminalization of homosexuality in late 2013, continue to discourage MTH community members from accessing health services. Pehchan has established Crisis Response Teams to support victims of violence and launched a national advocacy campaign for decriminalization. The program also addresses HIV stigma within MTH communities through outreach and counseling efforts. Pehchan’s comprehensive approach to capacity building, systems strengthening, and community mobilization has been effective and adaptable to other contexts where sexual minority communities are underserved. LVCT Health in Kenya provides essential services to MSM and sex workers outside traditional settings and schedules to overcome barriers to care. The program is peer-led and involves communities at all stages of the program cycle. Hotspots were mapped with community leaders and service providers to ensure non-judgmental and appropriate services. Focus group discussions and client exit interviews informed the program design. Engagement with bar owners and staff facilitated the availability of condoms and lubricants. Clients diagnosed with HIV through LVCT Health testing services are linked to treatment and care. Data on HIV risk factors, STI types, and HIV status are entered into a national database for trend analysis. Female sex workers receive routine STI and cervical cancer screening, with immediate diagnosis and referral for further management. Male sex workers are screened for STIs and lesions, offered syndromic management, and followed up in facility settings. LVCT Health reaches approximately 5,000 key population clients annually, with over 80% of HIV-positive clients effectively linked to post-test services. The program has achieved over 85% retention in care and treatment for MSM and over 90% adherence to HAART. Advocacy efforts have led to the inclusion of key population issues in Kenya’s HIV National Strategic Plan, enabling potential national-scale service delivery. Collaboration with the Ministry of Health and security agencies ensures service provision in insecure locations while maintaining staff and client safety. The National Organization of Peer Educators (NOPE) in Kenya developed the Drop-In Service Centre (DiSC) model as a one-stop approach for delivering essential HIV services to female sex workers and MSM in Kisii and Kiambu counties. Consultations and focus group discussions with these communities identified service gaps, followed by social and hotspot mapping and population size estimations. Stakeholder meetings, including bar owners, police, administrators, religious leaders, and community representatives, provided project information and encouraged community buy-in. Peer educators were trained to manage DiSCs, including setup, client flow, referral pathways, and minimum service packages. NOPE collaborated with District Health Management Teams for commodity sourcing and quality assurance. Routine data quality assessments, supervision visits, and progress meetings ensure robust monitoring and evaluation. DiSCs have served 20,000 individuals from FSW and MSM communities. NOPE’s experience has informed national guidelines for key populations and contributed to the development of a national MSM peer education curriculum. Technical assistance from NOPE has enabled other organizations to manage DiSCs. Building trust with key populations is critical, especially in environments where laws criminalize their behaviors. While standalone facilities are essential, integrating services into national health systems is necessary for sustainability. NOPE has mobilized county health teams to provide medical supplies and staff to DiSCs. The Marsa Sexual Health Centre in Beirut offers sexual and reproductive health services in a stigma-free environment, targeting young people, unmarried sexually active women, and marginalized communities, including MSM and transgender individuals. Anonymity and confidentiality are prioritized, with clients identified by unique file numbers. Staff are trained to maintain confidentiality, fostering trust and openness among clients. Marsa uses social media, the internet, street outreach, and word-of-mouth to share information about its services. Médecins du Monde (MdM) in Myanmar provides STI and HIV prevention, treatment, care, and harm reduction services for female sex workers, MSM, and people who use drugs. Services are offered free of charge at drop-in centers and clinics. The program was developed in collaboration with target populations, with peers playing a crucial role in ensuring the program meets their needs. Education, information, and supplies build trust, encouraging individuals to access more services. Strong relationships with local authorities influence operational frameworks and evidence-based policies. While HIV prevalence among key populations has decreased, rural areas with limited primary healthcare access pose challenges. MdM emphasizes addressing basic health needs alongside those of key populations to strengthen program acceptance and reduce misunderstandings. The organization aims to empower local NGOs and community-based groups to take over harm reduction efforts currently dependent on international NGOs. Skills transfer and capacity building are priorities in Myanmar. The Naz Male Health Alliance (NMHA) in Pakistan addresses the health and psychosocial needs of young MSM and transgender individuals through six service delivery centers in five cities, serving 47,000 registered clients. Each site includes a clinic and drop-in center, providing a safe environment for low-income MSM and transgender clients. Centers are strategically located near MSM hotspots and hijra deras. Drop-in centers establish long-term client relationships, while outreach links clients to services. Separate service sites cater to specific key population groups. Multidisciplinary teams, primarily community members, include physicians, psychologists, and peer educators. Over 95% of staff are MSM or transgender individuals. NMHA’s work has been publicly recognized by the Government of Pakistan.
